metadata.title: Three Scores Are Not Yet Three Chances
metadata.author: Aravind Sundaravadivelu
metadata.note: One concept: why three scores are not yet three chances. Every number on screen comes from evidence/softmax_steps_output.txt and evidence/main_py_output.txt (Python 3.12.14). The scores are constructed (chosen by hand). Divide-by-sum values are shown only as a contrast and are labelled as not the lesson's rule. Narration is a synthetic Kokoro voice (am_onyx); it is not the author, the instructor, or an endorsement. No Claude responses are shown.

beats.narration_text: Three scores: one, two, and three. I picked them by hand. No model produced them. A language model ends every step with numbers like these, one for each possible next token. It is tempting to read them as chances. They are not. Not yet.
beats.visual_intent: Three large score cards [1, 2, 3] with outcome labels 0, 1, 2 and a 'constructed input' tag; the question 'Are these three chances?' lands; synthetic-narration disclosure in the footer.

show.event: cards 1, 2, 3 rise in with outcome labels 0, 1, 2
tag: constructed input, chosen by hand, no model produced these

show.at: tempting to read them as chances
show.event: question 'Are these three chances?' appears; answer 'Not yet.' lands

beats.narration_text: Scores only rank the outcomes. To turn them into chances, you exponentiate the gaps between them, then divide by the total. That one move is the whole idea, and it comes with a limit worth naming.
beats.visual_intent: Hesitant writer: types 'Three scores are three chances.', greys out and deletes 'are three chances', retypes 'only rank three outcomes.'; the method line and the limit line follow.

show.event: types the misconception 'Three scores are three chances.'
wrong phrase greys out, is deleted, and is replaced by 'only rank three outcomes.'
second line types: chances = exponentiate the gaps, divide by the total
third line: '...and it has a limit.'

beats.narration_text: The obvious fix is to divide by the sum. For one, two, three the sum is six, which gives a sixth, a third, and a half. That looks fine. But scores can be negative. Minus one, two, three gives a chance below zero. Minus one, zero, one divides by zero. The rule we want has to survive any finite score.
beats.visual_intent: Three rows of divide-by-sum: [1,2,3]/6 -> [0.1667, 0.3333, 0.5000] marked OK; [-1,2,3]/4 -> [-0.2500, ...] marked with the negative value boxed; [-1,0,1]/0 -> ZeroDivisionError. Label: divide-by-sum is not the lesson's rule.

show.event: row 2: [-1, 2, 3] / 4, the -0.2500 is boxed as 'chance below zero'
footer: divide-by-sum is NOT the lesson's rule

beats.narration_text: Here is the lesson's actual function. It makes three moves. Find the largest score and subtract it from every score. Exponentiate each result. Then divide every weight by the total. Temperature stays at one for this whole video. That knob is a different story.
beats.visual_intent: The real probabilities() source from main.py (lines 9-17); three lines get numbered callouts 1, 2, 3 on the spoken moves; temperature note.

show.event: code block of main.py lines 9-17 fades in with file path
callout 1 boxes 'peak = max(logits)' and the subtraction

beats.narration_text: Run it on one, two, three. Subtract the peak, three, and the scores become minus two, minus one, and zero. Exponentiate: zero point one three five, zero point three six eight, and exactly one. Every weight is now positive. Add them up: one point five zero three. Divide each weight by that total, and the chances are zero point zero nine zero, zero point two four five, and zero point six six five. They sum to one.
beats.visual_intent: Five columns revealed left to right with the real values: SCORES [1,2,3] -> MINUS PEAK [-2,-1,0] -> EXP [0.1353,0.3679,1.0000] -> TOTAL 1.5032 -> CHANCES [0.0900,0.2447,0.6652] with bars; 'sum = 1.0000'.

beats.narration_text: Here is what the exponent is really doing. Each one point step in score multiplies the weight by e, about two point seven one eight. Dividing by the total cannot undo that, because every weight is divided by the same number. So each chance is two point seven one eight times the one below it. The gaps set the ratios. Divide by six instead, and that ratio is one point five. A different rule.
beats.visual_intent: Weights row with 'x 2.7183' hops between neighbours; the same hops reappear on the chances row; a small contrast panel shows divide-by-sum's ratio 1.5000.

show.at: each chance is two point seven one eight times

beats.narration_text: Now the input that broke division: minus one, two, three. The lesson's function handles it. Minus one becomes a tiny positive weight, and the chances come out zero point zero one three, zero point two six five, and zero point seven two one. All positive, summing to one. A gap of three points multiplies by e cubed, about twenty. The biggest score still gets the biggest chance.
beats.visual_intent: [-1, 2, 3] through probabilities(): MINUS PEAK [-4,-1,0] -> WEIGHTS [0.0183,0.3679,1.0000] -> CHANCES [0.0132,0.2654,0.7214] with bars; divide-by-sum's -0.2500 shown crossed out as the comparison; annotation 'gap 3 -> x 20.0855 = e cubed'.

beats.narration_text: Here is what this does not establish. These are chances of being sampled from my three hand-picked scores. They are not chances of being right. In exact arithmetic, the transformation guarantees positive numbers that sum to one and keep the scores' order. It says nothing about whether the scores were sensible, or whether outcome two is true. A confident distribution can still be confidently wrong.
beats.visual_intent: Bars [0.0900, 0.2447, 0.6652] labelled 'chance of being SAMPLED'; beside them a checklist: guaranteed (positive, sums to 1, order kept) versus NOT established (scores sensible? outcome 2 true? calibrated?).

show.event: 'chance of being right' appears greyed with 'not shown'

beats.narration_text: So, three scores are not yet three chances. Exponentiate the gaps, divide by the total, and you get a distribution that keeps the order and every ratio. Your turn: before you run it, predict the chances for one, two, and four.
